title: Multidimensional control of surface acoustic wave generation via programmable interdigital transducer arrays

paper_content.abstract: Fixed interdigital transducers (IDTs) are commonly limited to only generate a single type of surface acoustic wave (SAW). Here, we present a programmable IDT array architecture for multidimensional SAW generation, based on standard and chirped IDT array designs. Forty independently addressable IDT units are each modulated by a double-pole-double-throw switch to enable binary phase inversion. This system generates diverse SAW waveforms including non-diffracting Airy SAWs and dynamically focused SAWs. We achieve two-dimensional focus manipulation with sub-wavelength precision and extended focal depth, enabled by time-division multiplexing with chirped IDTs. By combining spatial phase encoding with spectral frequency multiplexing, our approach demonstrates multidimensional control over SAW generation, providing a platform for adaptive acoustic field control in applications such as reconfigurable microfluidics, tuneable metamaterials, and multifrequency sensing systems.
paper_content.introduction:
Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are mechanical waves that propagate along the surface of a solid material, with their amplitudes decaying exponentially into the bulk. Since their first observation by Lord Rayleigh in 1885 [1], SAWs have been widely utilized across various fields. In modern applications, SAWs are primarily generated using interdigital transducers (IDTs) deposited on piezoelectric substrates. By exploiting the inverse piezoelectric effect, an applied electric potential across the IDTs is converted into mechanical energy, producing SAWs that propagate along the substrate's surface. The unique properties of SAWs, such as low energy consumption, high sensitivity, and compatibility with integrated circuit technology, have facilitated their extensive applications in sensors [2−4], filters [5−7], acoustic microfluidics [8−12], particles manipulation [13−18], among others. Although conventional SAW devices with fixed geometries are the cornerstone of major applications such as radio frequency (RF) filters and stable sensor platforms, they lack the dynamic reconfigurability or programmability required for booming applications in microfluidics and particle manipulation. Therefore, the development of dynamically modulated SAWs is essential to address the evolving requirements in modern technologies and intricate operational environments.

Currently, SAW modulation is primarily achieved through two distinct approaches. The first involves the integration of tailored metastructures onto a pre-existing SAW wavefront [19−23]. As SAWs propagate through these metastructures, their phase or amplitude is modulated, thereby alerting their morphological characteristics. This method offers high flexibility, enabling precise control over SAWs and waveguiding [24] by adjusting the dimensions, arrangement, and defects within the metastructure units. However, strong wave attenuation occurs upon interaction with these structures, and their fabrication remains complex. The second approach modifies the geometric configuration and arrangement of the IDT fingers to achieve the various SAW characteristics, such as slanted-finger IDTs [25,26], focused IDTs [27,28], chirped IDTs [29,30], multiple IDTs [31,32], and IDT arrays [33]. This method simplifies fabrication and improves energy conversion efficiency, enhancing the overall performance and reliability of SAW devices. While recent programmable IDT platforms [31–33] have demonstrated the ability to generate arbitrary wavefields, they typically rely on multi-channel driving architectures with independently controlled inputs, which increase system-level hardware complexity compared to single-input solutions. The practical deployment of such multi-input systems is often hindered by their inherent hardware complexity and the need for precise synchronization of multiple channels, posing a potential barrier to their broader adoption.

To overcome this limitation, we report an innovative approach for multidimensionally controlled SAWs generation using a programmable IDT array, enabling both efficient generation and flexible modulation of multiple waveforms through phase and frequency tuning. By integrating an externally controlled encoding circuit, each IDT unit within the array operates independently, allowing for precise phase transitions via a switching mechanism. Additionally, a programmable chirped IDT array is introduced to generate multifrequency SAWs, where gradually varying electrode widths enable tailored frequency responses. Time-division multiplexing (TDM) is employed to enable concurrent signal transmission by allocating distinct time slots to individual data streams within a shared channel [34−36]. This technique sequentially samples multiple signals, assigns each to brief, non-overlapping temporal windows, and reconstructs them at the receiver through synchronized decoding. The chirped IDT array leverages TDM to superimpose multifrequency SAWs through temporally encoded excitations, generating tailored focused acoustic fields—the so-called “SAW needle”—for advanced microfluidic and sensing applications. Furthermore, two-dimensional manipulation of particles is demonstrated through the encoded switching control of IDTs arranged in a one-dimensional configuration. The proposed multidimensional SAW modulation approach offers several advantages, including simplified fabrication, enhanced regulatory flexibility, and highly reduced acoustic energy attenuation. These attributes render the SAW devices highly efficient and adaptable for a wide range of applications in acoustic wave-based technologies.
paper_content.results:
Programmable IDT Array Design. In our design, both standard and chirped IDT configuration are miniaturized laterally to form individual IDT unit, each capable of discrete control. An IDT array is assembled by arranging these identical units in parallel, with their corresponding electrode pins. The fabricated IDT array is patterned onto a lithium niobate (LiNbO ) wafer using the photolithography technique. To enable selective control, the electrode pins of the IDT array are connected to a control circuit via a flat flexible cable (FFC), allowing each IDT unit to be independently modulated through discrete switches integrated within the control module. This configuration provides precise phase and frequency control over the generated SAWs. The generation and modulation of multidimensional SAWs are achieved through sequentially encoded control of the discrete switches. The resultant acoustic field distribution is characterized by a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) with the laser beam focused on the surface of the LiNbO wafer, as shown in Fig. 1a.

To ensure compatibility with the FFC, the electrode pins extracted from this array are arranged in a uniform lateral spacing configuration. Full details on the standard and chirped IDT arrays are described in Supplementary Note 1. Each IDT unit has a pair of electrode pins, resulting in a total of 80 pins for the entire array. After post-extension, these 80 pins are aligned in a uniform, equidistant manner, with spacing of 500 µm. Each pin has a width of 250 µm and a length of 4 mm, as shown in Fig. 1b.

The individual IDT unit is controlled by a double pole double throw (DPDT) switch, as illustrated in Fig. 1c. To ensure the system stability under amplified voltages (>50 V), relatively high frequencies (>7 MHz) and prolonged operation (>8 hrs), a manually controlled DPDT switch was selected in the experiment. The dual pins emanating from the IDT unit are affixed to the respective terminals C and D of the DPDT switch. The input signal, maintained at a floating potential, is applied to terminals A and F, while terminals B and E are grounded. By toggling the DPDT switch, terminals C and D can be connected either to A and B, or to E and F. This switching mechanism enables inversion of the electrical potential across the IDT unit, effectively inducing the phase-inversion in the generated SAW. This binary modulation of the wave’s phase is referred to as “1” for the initial phase state and “0” for the phase-inverted state. Consequently, this programmable phase modulation provides a versatile and efficient means of dynamically controlling SAW properties, facilitating precise wave manipulation for various applications. The detailed fabrication and integration processes for the SAW device with the standard and chirped IDTs are comprehensively described in Supplementary Note 2.

Phase and Frequency Validation. The core mechanism in this work is based on the superposition of SAWs generated by each individual IDT unit. To effectively control the wavefront of the resultant SAW, it is essential to establish phase coherence among the individual SAW through the modulation of DPDT switches. In our experiment, the superpositioned SAW was synchronized with the signal generator and analyzed using the LDV measurements. The implementation details regarding the experimental setup are provided in Supplementary Note 3. Distinct SAW signals emitted by the IDT unit under the two switching states, “1” and “0” of the DPDT switch are demonstrated in Fig. 2a. The time-domain signals corresponding to these states exhibit an exact phase difference of π, confirming that the SAWs generated from individual IDT units can be modulated in a binary phase manner by toggling the DPDT switch. This capability enables precise phase control, which is fundamental for achieving programmable wavefront manipulation.

To evaluate the frequency response of the chirped IDT array, a frequency sweep measurement was performed. All control module states were initially set to “1” to maintain phase uniformity across the chirped IDT units, thereby generating planar SAWs. Multiple measurements were taken at different points and averaged to minimize experimental errors. The collected data were subsequently smoothed and normalized, producing the frequency response curve shown in Fig. 2b. The results indicate that the chirped IDT array exhibits a broadband response, with activity between 6.58 MHz and 9.45 MHz. It is worth noting that the multiple peaks observed in Fig. 2b originate not from structural resonances, but Fresnel ripples—an inherent feature of any finite-length, broadband chirp signal in both time and frequency domains [37]. Within this range, Fresnel ripple peaks were identified at f = 7.20 MHz, f = 7.81 MHz, f = 8.35 MHz, and f = 8.78 MHz. This analysis provides a comprehensive characterization of the array’s frequency response, forming a foundation for future multifrequency modulation and applications.

Additionally, for the chirped IDT array comprising 40 units separated by a fixed gap, ensuring the continuity and smoothness of the superpositioned SAW is crucial. A detailed LDV scan was conducted with the starting point at ~3 mm away from the chirped IDT array along the SAW propagation path. The scanning area was 2 mm × 1 mm with a step size of 20 µm. The scanned results of planar SAWs at the four Fresnel ripple peak frequencies from f to f are illustrated in Fig. 2c−f. The x-direction scan spans 1 mm, covering approximately 5 IDT units, while the y-direction scan spans 2 mm, which corresponds to approximately 4𝜆 of the SAWs. As shown in Fig. 2c−f, no obvious misalignment was observed between the SAWs generated by discrete IDT units, confirming that their wavefronts remain collinear. Furthermore, the amplitude of the generated SAWs is uniform, with negligible fluctuations. According to the Huygens–Fresnel principle, each individual unit can be regarded as a point source radiating the secondary wavelet. When multiple units are arranged in close proximity with the interunit gap (10 µm) much smaller than the wavelength (500 µm), the coherent superposition of the secondary wavelets results in a stable, uniform primary wavefront. The minimal interunit gap reduces acoustic energy loss, facilitating the coherent superposition of SAWs from adjacent IDT units. Furthermore, when the input signals to the IDT units are out-of-phase, the corresponding secondary wavelets also maintain a consistent anti-phase relationship, which has been discussed in our previous work [38].

SAW Waveform Modulation. In the standard IDT array, each individual IDT unit enables binary phase modulation of the SAW through the control of its corresponding DPDT switch. By programmably encoding the phase states of the SAWs generated by each IDT unit, various types of the superpositioned SAWs can be achieved, tailored for specific acoustic wave manipulation and control applications. As a demonstration, we generated Airy-type SAWs using the programmable IDT array. Following a similar phase design in our previous work [38], we binarized the Airy function [39], assigning a phase value of 𝜋 to amplitudes greater than 0 and a value of 0 to amplitudes less than 0 [40,41], as depicted in Fig. 3a. The binarized Airy function was then correlated with the spatial phase distribution of the IDT units. Given the limited number of the IDT units (only 40) in our experiment, the number of units assigned to each individual binarized state is illustrated in Fig. 3b. Experiments and simulations were conducted within a 4 cm  2 cm area in front of the IDT array, covering the SAW propagation zone. The experimental and simulation results are shown in Fig. 3c−f, respectively. For clarity, the IDT arrays generating Airy SAWs are highlighted in Fig. 3c and e, with black and white blocks representing the states “1” and “0”, respectively. The digit within each block indicates the number of the IDT units assigned to each state. To simplify the encoding representation, adjacent digits in the sequence correspond to binarized phases 0 and . In Fig. 3c and e, the digit sequences “7, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2” and “2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 7” indicate the arrangement of the IDT unit from the bottom to the top. Upon activation of the IDT array, the generated SAW’s acoustic field was scanned using the LDV. The resulting acoustic field distributions, shown in Fig. 3c and e, exhibit the characteristics bending trajectory of the Airy SAW. Notably, the Airy SAWs in Fig. 3c and e bend in opposite directions due to the reversed digit sequences, confirming the programmable nature of our approach. The corresponding simulation results in Fig. 3d and f closely match the experimental observations validate the accuracy of our encoding method. This programmability offers great flexibility in generating various types of SAWs, expanding potential applications in acoustic wave engineering and related fields. Detailed information regarding the simulation model and parameter settings can be found in Supplementary Note 4.

Spatially Focal Positioning Modulation. The superposition of the curved main lobes from two symmetrical Airy SAWs can generate a focused acoustic field. By positioning two co-axial standard IDT arrays in opposite orientations, a focused standing SAW is formed. In our experiment, we mapped a 2 cm × 1 cm area between the two IDT arrays using the LDV for detailed analysis. The predefined digit sequences encoded in the IDT arrays allow for vertical control of the focal point within the focused standing SAW.

The scanned acoustic field distribution reveals the characteristics of the focused SAW, as shown in Fig. 4a. The encoded digit sequences for both IDT arrays in Fig. 4a are “3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2”. The rationale for the encoded digit sequences can be found in Supplementary Note 5. A distinct focusing effect is observed, with the focal region appearing elongated along the wave propagation direction (x-direction), indicating a notable depth of focus. In contrast, the focal width (lateral resolution) in the perpendicular direction (y-direction) is much narrower. This focused acoustic field forms the basis for controlling particle movement along the y-direction in subsequent experiments. To achieve focal point shifting, the encoding sequence was adjusted by shifting 4 IDT units in the -y direction. The new sequences “2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2” and “2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3,” successfully moved the focal point downward, as demonstrated in Fig. 4b and c. The results show a consistent downward shift of the focal point while maintaining lateral position and focal depth. By extracting the acoustic field distributions along dashed lines A, B, and C, the measured focal displacements d and d were 0.88 mm and 0.96 mm, respectively, closely aligning with the theoretical displacement of 0.92 mm (4 units × 0.23 mm). Simulated acoustic fields (Fig. 4e−g) further validated these findings, with simulated focal displacements l and l measured at 0.9 mm, shown in Fig. 4h. These results confirm that modifying the IDT array encoding sequence enables precise focal point control in the y-direction.

Theoretically, the number of the central IDT units determines the initial position of the main lobe of the Airy SAW and, consequently, the focal point position of the combined focused SAW [42]. To validate this, we altered the encoding sequences to induce lateral focus shifts. The left-side IDT digit sequence was set to “2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2,” while the right-side sequence was “2, 3, 3, 4, 16, 4, 3, 3, 2,” resulting in a leftward focal shift, as shown in Fig. 5a. This shift occurred because fewer central units on the left generated a shorter focal length, while the increased number of units on the right produced a longer focal length. When both sides were symmetrically encoded with the digit sequence “2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2,” the focal lengths became equal, centering the focal point, as shown in Fig. 5b. Reversing the asymmetry—setting the left and right sequences to “2, 3, 3, 4, 16, 4, 3, 3, 2” and “2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2,” respectively—resulted in a rightward focal shift, symmetric to the first case (Fig. 5c). Cross-sectional acoustic field distributions extracted along dashed lines A, B, and C from Fig. 5a−c, shown in Fig. 5d, indicate focal displacements d₁ and d₂ of approximately 3.91 mm and 3.8 mm, respectively, which closely match the design values. Corresponding simulations (Fig. 5e−g) confirm these results, demonstrating consistent focal shifts. The cross-sectional acoustic intensities along the x-direction (Fig. 5h) reveal lateral displacements l₁ and l₂ of approximately 4 mm, further aligning with the experimental observations. Such dynamic focal position manipulation enabled by programmable IDT array coding can be used for controlled particle movement. The working principle for the particle control and corresponding experimental demonstration are discussed in Supplementary Note 6.

Multifrequency Focal Depth Modulation. By modifying the chirped IDT array’s encoding, with the digit sequence “2, 3, 3, 4, 16, 4, 3, 3, 2”, a focused SAW is generated. The acoustic field distributions of the focused SAWs at four different frequencies were scanned using LDV over a 1.5 cm × 2.5 cm propagation area, with the results shown in Fig. 6a−d. At the frequency of f , the generated SAW exhibits a strong focusing effect, forming an elongated focal spot near the chirped IDT array, as depicted in Fig. 6a. As the frequency increases to f , the focus shifts along the +x direction while maintaining focusing characteristics, as shown in Fig. 6b. At the frequency of f , the focal point shifts along the +x direction, as shown in Fig. 6c. Finally, at the frequency of f , the focal point reaches its farthest position from the IDT array, meanwhile still exhibiting a distinct focusing effect, as seen in Fig. 6d. These results demonstrate that the focus position can be effectively controlled by adjusting the excitation frequency. Cross-sectional profiles along the y- and x-direction at the focal points, indicated by white dashed lines in Fig. 6a−d, are analyzed with the results shown in Fig. 6e and f, respectively. The amplitude values are normalized to the maximum at the focal point. The acoustic field distribution along the y-direction (Fig. 6e) reveals that the focal points at all frequencies overlap, with a focal width of approximately 2𝜆, indicating consistent focus positioning and excellent symmetry. In contrast, along the x-direction (Fig. 6f), the focal position shifts farther from the chirped IDT array as the frequency increases, reaching a maximum displacement of approximately 11 mm. The average full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the focal depth along the x-direction was measured individually for each operating frequency. The obtained values are as follows: 22𝜆 at f₁ = 7.20 MHz, 29𝜆 at f₂ = 7.81 MHz, 28𝜆 at f₃ = 8.35 MHz, and 28𝜆 at f₄ = 8.78 MHz, respectively. This confirms the strong frequency dependence of SAW focusing, enabling precise control over the focal position through frequency tunning. This approach provides a tunable method for concentrating acoustic energy at specific locations, which is highly beneficial for practical applications.

The frequency-dependent focal position of focused SAWs generated by two primary mechanisms. First, within the chirped IDT array, designed with progressively wider finger widths, the generated SAWs with different frequencies are position-dependent: the activation regions for lower and higher frequency SAWs are at the rear and front of the chirped IDT array, respectively. Second, focused SAWs arise from the superposition of symmetric main lobes of Airy SAWs. At higher frequencies, reduced acceleration and main lobe curvature push the focal point further from the source. Together, these mechanisms enable precise frequency-based control of the focal position.

To validate the modulation effect of multi-frequency excitation on the focused SAW, the TDM technique was applied to temporally concatenate four discrete Fresnel ripple peak frequencies, thereby generating TDM waveforms. The technical implementation scheme and corresponding spatial-temporal modulation characteristics are analyzed in Supplementary Note 7. The TDM is generated using MATLAB, and the corresponding code is provided in Supplementary Note 8. The location of the focused energy along the x-axis varies with the operating frequency, as shown in Fig. 6f. The SAW with a higher frequency has a longer focal length from the excitation source. The focal positions of SAWs vary with excitation frequency, leading to distinct energy distributions at each focal point when multifrequency components are superimposed. By adjusting the relative contributions of different frequencies, the focusing effect can be sustained across an extended propagation distance, thereby increasing the focal depth. Since the generated SAWs with frequencies of f₁ (7.20 MHz) and f₄ (8.78 MHz) have the nearest and farthest focal points, respectively, their signal weighting should be enhanced. Meanwhile, the generated SAWs with frequencies of f₂ (7.81 MHz) and f₃ (8.35 MHz) have the focused energy distributions that overlap with those of f₁ and f₄ to a large extent. Therefore, their relative contributions should be minimized to achieve a more uniform energy distribution along the x-axis across the four frequencies, thus extending the effective focal depth. A reference TDM signal with equal cycle allocations (f : f : f : f = 5:5:5:5) serves as a baseline configuration, where each ratio value indicates the number of wavelength cycles per frequency component. LDV scans over a 15 mm × 40 mm propagation area mapped the acoustic field distributions for various TDM configurations (Fig. 7a−e). All tested frequency ratios maintained strong focusing performance while demonstrating progressive focal depth extension. Cross-sectional intensity profiles along the propagation direction (x-axis) extracted from Fig. 7, enable quantitative comparison of focal depth variations across TDM configurations (Fig. 8). These profiles permit systematic evaluation of both focal depth and axial energy distribution for each frequency ratio combination.

The relationship between TDM signal composition and focal depth is quantified using FWHM analysis of the acoustic field profiles, as shown in Fig. 8. Increasing the proportion of f (8.78 MHz) from the baseline (5:5:5:5) to an optimized configuration (5:0:4:11) ratios results in the focal depth extension from 40λ to 43λ by temporally stitching the acoustic fields of generated SAWs with different frequencies. However, excessive f weighting reduces the focal depth to 27λ due to diminished near-field contributions from f (7.20 MHz). This nonlinear behavior results from unbalanced energy distribution: a dominant f components amplifies distal focusing but weakens proximal intensity, disrupting superposition across the extended focal depth. For the frequency combination of (5:0:4:11), the SAW energy assigned to the frequency of f₂ is 0, meaning that the f₂-frequency SAW has no contribution. This is likely because the f₂-frequency SAW energy distribution overlaps with those of f₁ and f₃, while its peak is higher than that of f₃ (see Fig. 6f). Therefore, to extend the focal depth, our proposed frequency-weighting strategy is to suppress f₂ and f₃ while increase f₄. As a result, we experimentally optimized (5:0:4:11) ratio to achieve the extended focal depth of 43λ with uniform energy distribution.
paper_content.methods:
Simulation. Numerical simulations were performed using the Piezoelectricity module in COMSOL Multiphysics. A two-dimensional model of a 128° Y-X cut LiNbO₃ substrate was constructed to reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy. Perfectly matched layers (PMLs) with a thickness of approximately one wavelength (500 μm) were applied around the substrate to absorb boundary reflections. The IDT array electrodes were modelled on the substrate surface and excited with either in-phase or out-of-phase voltage signals (20 Vₚₚ) to control the acoustic phase. The resulting acoustic field distributions were visualized by plotting the displacement field.

Experiment. The IDT arrays were fabricated on a 128° Y-X cut LiNbO₃ substrate using standard photolithography, followed by deposition of a 3-nm Cr adhesion layer and a 50-nm Au electrode layer via electron beam evaporation. The arrays consist of 40 independently addressable IDT units, each connected to a control module equipped with DPDT switches for binary phase inversion. SAWs were generated by applying AC signals (20 Vₚₚ, 7.98 MHz for standard IDTs; 5–12 MHz swept for chirped IDTs) from a signal generator (DG4102, Rigol, China). The out-of-plane displacement fields of propagating SAWs were measured using a LDV (PSV-500 Scanning Head, Polytec, Germany). The entire setup was mounted on a two-axis stepper motor translation stage with 10 μm positioning resolution.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Article title : « Multidimensionally Controlled Surface Acoustic Waves Generation via Programmable Interdigital Transducer
Arrays »
What are the noteworthy results?
This study addresses the generation of two-dimensionally controlled surface acoustic waves (SAWs) using a programmable
interdigital transducer (IDT) array. The authors developed both a single-frequency and a broadband chirped IDT system with
an aperture of 8.8 mm. The aperture is segmented into 40 parallel emitting units, each capable of on-demand phase
inversion using double-pole double-throw (DPDT) switches. This 1-bit phase modulation of SAW emission wavefront
enabled the generation of non-diffracting Airy SAWs and dynamically focused wavefronts. Furthermore, by incorporating
time-division multiplexing (TDM) with the chirped IDT array, the authors achieved extended focal depth.
Currently, the switches are operated manually, but the approach is amenable to automation. The system requires only a
single-channel arbitrary waveform generator, and the fabrication of the IDT array is relatively simple.
Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature?
The work is of potential interest to the microfluidics and acoustic manipulation communities. Although programmable IDT
concepts have been previously explored, their representation in the literature remains limited, and the authors' overview
generally reflects the current state. Nevertheless, the following reference should be added to improve completeness: DOI:
10.1039/c9lc00465c. Given the modest requirements of the presented platform in terms of equipment and processing, the
approach offers a resource-efficient alternative to more complex programmable IDT systems.
One of the central statements in the introduction may require revision for accuracy:
“Despite their advantages, both approaches share the same fundamental limitation: once metastructures or IDTs are
fabricated, they can generate only a single type of SAWs, lacking the flexibility to produce diverse waveforms within a single
device.”
This statement is not universally applicable. Systems presented in [31, 32] are capable of generating arbitrary SAW fields
within a single device (e.g., plane waves of arbitrary direction, focused beams, etc.). While it is true that the present approach
offers advantages in implementation simplicity and hardware requirements, the claim should be reformulated to reflect the
actual limitations more accurately.
Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
The experimental data, which include simulations, laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV) measurements and particle manipulation
videos, support the authors’ conclusions.
Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? - Do these prohibit publication or require revision?
Although the main results are substantiated, the manuscript would benefit from improved consistency in presentation and
terminology. For example, the use of the term “resonant frequencies” for the chirped IDT is problematic:
Lines 158–159:
The statement “Fig. 2c–f presents the scanned results of planar SAWs at the four resonant frequencies” should be revised.
The IDT used in the experiment is a hyperbolic-type chirped transducer, which operates over a broad frequency range and
does not exhibit discrete resonances in the conventional sense.
Figure below represents time and frequency-domain impulse response of the chirped transduces as described in
Supplementary Note 1. The spectral peaks observed in the impulse response and the corresponding local maxima in the
LDV measurements are not due to resonant behavior but rather arise from interference effects associated with the
broadband excitation. These features are consistent with Fresnel ripples, as described in [https://doi.org/10.1049/ip-f-
1.1980.0018]. Such ripples are characteristic of broadband, spatially modulated emission and do not reflect intrinsic
resonant properties of the structure.
The authors are advised to refer to these frequencies as “frequencies corresponding to Fresnel ripples” instead of “resonant
frequencies,” and to explicitly state that a hyperbolic-type chirped IDT is employed.

Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
In general, the overall idea is interesting, but several important issues remain:
• The limitations of the approach (insertion loss, attenuation, etc.) are not discussed.
• There is no comparison with existing methods in the literature.
Other issues could be cites as follows:
• Possible thermal effects or power limits to avoid IDT degradation are not addressed. In the demonstration video, did you
quantify the power required to move the particles? Did you observe any thermal effects? Is there a power limit beyond which
the IDTs could degrade?
• The MATLAB code used to generate the TDM signal is not shared or referenced.
• No data on absolute SAW displacements is given.
• The coupling effect between the IDTs is not considered.
• No quantitative data on the power required to move the particles is provided, despite the demonstration video.

In general, yes. However:
• No insight into how programming sequences (like “2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2”) other than the first one are provided.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question, which gets to the very heart of

of the primary sources (the array elements) to dictate the outcome of this
interference.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Fixed interdigital transducers (IDTs) are commonly limited to only generate a single type of surface acoustic wave (SAW). Here, we present a programmable IDT array architecture for multidimensional SAW generation, based on standard and chirped IDT array designs. Forty independently addressable IDT units are each modulated by a double-pole-double-throw switch to enable binary phase inversion. This system generates diverse SAW waveforms including non-diffracting Airy SAWs and dynamically focused SAWs. We achieve two-dimensional focus manipulation with sub-wavelength precision and extended focal depth, enabled by time-division multiplexing with chirped IDTs. By combining spatial phase encoding with spectral frequency multiplexing, our approach demonstrates multidimensional control over SAW generation, providing a platform for adaptive acoustic field control in applications such as reconfigurable microfluidics, tuneable metamaterials, and multifrequency sensing systems.

---

## Introduction

Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are mechanical waves that propagate along the surface of a solid material, with their amplitudes decaying exponentially into the bulk. Since their first observation by Lord Rayleigh in 1885 [1], SAWs have been widely utilized across various fields. In modern applications, SAWs are primarily generated using interdigital transducers (IDTs) deposited on piezoelectric substrates. By exploiting the inverse piezoelectric effect, an applied electric potential across the IDTs is converted into mechanical energy, producing SAWs that propagate along the substrate's surface. The unique properties of SAWs, such as low energy consumption, high sensitivity, and compatibility with integrated circuit technology, have facilitated their extensive applications in sensors [2−4], filters [5−7], acoustic microfluidics [8−12], particles manipulation [13−18], among others. Although conventional SAW devices with fixed geometries are the cornerstone of major applications such as radio frequency (RF) filters and stable sensor platforms, they lack the dynamic reconfigurability or programmability required for booming applications in microfluidics and particle manipulation. Therefore, the development of dynamically modulated SAWs is essential to address the evolving requirements in modern technologies and intricate operational environments.

Currently, SAW modulation is primarily achieved through two distinct approaches. The first involves the integration of tailored metastructures onto a pre-existing SAW wavefront [19−23]. As SAWs propagate through these metastructures, their phase or amplitude is modulated, thereby alerting their morphological characteristics. This method offers high flexibility, enabling precise control over SAWs and waveguiding [24] by adjusting the dimensions, arrangement, and defects within the metastructure units. However, strong wave attenuation occurs upon interaction with these structures, and their fabrication remains complex. The second approach modifies the geometric configuration and arrangement of the IDT fingers to achieve the various SAW characteristics, such as slanted-finger IDTs [25,26], focused IDTs [27,28], chirped IDTs [29,30], multiple IDTs [31,32], and IDT arrays [33]. This method simplifies fabrication and improves energy conversion efficiency, enhancing the overall performance and reliability of SAW devices. While recent programmable IDT platforms [31–33] have demonstrated the ability to generate arbitrary wavefields, they typically rely on multi-channel driving architectures with independently controlled inputs, which increase system-level hardware complexity compared to single-input solutions. The practical deployment of such multi-input systems is often hindered by their inherent hardware complexity and the need for precise synchronization of multiple channels, posing a potential barrier to their broader adoption.

To overcome this limitation, we report an innovative approach for multidimensionally controlled SAWs generation using a programmable IDT array, enabling both efficient generation and flexible modulation of multiple waveforms through phase and frequency tuning. By integrating an externally controlled encoding circuit, each IDT unit within the array operates independently, allowing for precise phase transitions via a switching mechanism. Additionally, a programmable chirped IDT array is introduced to generate multifrequency SAWs, where gradually varying electrode widths enable tailored frequency responses. Time-division multiplexing (TDM) is employed to enable concurrent signal transmission by allocating distinct time slots to individual data streams within a shared channel [34−36]. This technique sequentially samples multiple signals, assigns each to brief, non-overlapping temporal windows, and reconstructs them at the receiver through synchronized decoding. The chirped IDT array leverages TDM to superimpose multifrequency SAWs through temporally encoded excitations, generating tailored focused acoustic fields—the so-called “SAW needle”—for advanced microfluidic and sensing applications. Furthermore, two-dimensional manipulation of particles is demonstrated through the encoded switching control of IDTs arranged in a one-dimensional configuration. The proposed multidimensional SAW modulation approach offers several advantages, including simplified fabrication, enhanced regulatory flexibility, and highly reduced acoustic energy attenuation. These attributes render the SAW devices highly efficient and adaptable for a wide range of applications in acoustic wave-based technologies.

---

## Results

Programmable IDT Array Design. In our design, both standard and chirped IDT configuration are miniaturized laterally to form individual IDT unit, each capable of discrete control. An IDT array is assembled by arranging these identical units in parallel, with their corresponding electrode pins. The fabricated IDT array is patterned onto a lithium niobate (LiNbO ) wafer using the photolithography technique. To enable selective control, the electrode pins of the IDT array are connected to a control circuit via a flat flexible cable (FFC), allowing each IDT unit to be independently modulated through discrete switches integrated within the control module. This configuration provides precise phase and frequency control over the generated SAWs. The generation and modulation of multidimensional SAWs are achieved through sequentially encoded control of the discrete switches. The resultant acoustic field distribution is characterized by a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) with the laser beam focused on the surface of the LiNbO wafer, as shown in Fig. 1a.

To ensure compatibility with the FFC, the electrode pins extracted from this array are arranged in a uniform lateral spacing configuration. Full details on the standard and chirped IDT arrays are described in Supplementary Note 1. Each IDT unit has a pair of electrode pins, resulting in a total of 80 pins for the entire array. After post-extension, these 80 pins are aligned in a uniform, equidistant manner, with spacing of 500 µm. Each pin has a width of 250 µm and a length of 4 mm, as shown in Fig. 1b.

The individual IDT unit is controlled by a double pole double throw (DPDT) switch, as illustrated in Fig. 1c. To ensure the system stability under amplified voltages (>50 V), relatively high frequencies (>7 MHz) and prolonged operation (>8 hrs), a manually controlled DPDT switch was selected in the experiment. The dual pins emanating from the IDT unit are affixed to the respective terminals C and D of the DPDT switch. The input signal, maintained at a floating potential, is applied to terminals A and F, while terminals B and E are grounded. By toggling the DPDT switch, terminals C and D can be connected either to A and B, or to E and F. This switching mechanism enables inversion of the electrical potential across the IDT unit, effectively inducing the phase-inversion in the generated SAW. This binary modulation of the wave’s phase is referred to as “1” for the initial phase state and “0” for the phase-inverted state. Consequently, this programmable phase modulation provides a versatile and efficient means of dynamically controlling SAW properties, facilitating precise wave manipulation for various applications. The detailed fabrication and integration processes for the SAW device with the standard and chirped IDTs are comprehensively described in Supplementary Note 2.

Phase and Frequency Validation. The core mechanism in this work is based on the superposition of SAWs generated by each individual IDT unit. To effectively control the wavefront of the resultant SAW, it is essential to establish phase coherence among the individual SAW through the modulation of DPDT switches. In our experiment, the superpositioned SAW was synchronized with the signal generator and analyzed using the LDV measurements. The implementation details regarding the experimental setup are provided in Supplementary Note 3. Distinct SAW signals emitted by the IDT unit under the two switching states, “1” and “0” of the DPDT switch are demonstrated in Fig. 2a. The time-domain signals corresponding to these states exhibit an exact phase difference of π, confirming that the SAWs generated from individual IDT units can be modulated in a binary phase manner by toggling the DPDT switch. This capability enables precise phase control, which is fundamental for achieving programmable wavefront manipulation.

To evaluate the frequency response of the chirped IDT array, a frequency sweep measurement was performed. All control module states were initially set to “1” to maintain phase uniformity across the chirped IDT units, thereby generating planar SAWs. Multiple measurements were taken at different points and averaged to minimize experimental errors. The collected data were subsequently smoothed and normalized, producing the frequency response curve shown in Fig. 2b. The results indicate that the chirped IDT array exhibits a broadband response, with activity between 6.58 MHz and 9.45 MHz. It is worth noting that the multiple peaks observed in Fig. 2b originate not from structural resonances, but Fresnel ripples—an inherent feature of any finite-length, broadband chirp signal in both time and frequency domains [37]. Within this range, Fresnel ripple peaks were identified at f = 7.20 MHz, f = 7.81 MHz, f = 8.35 MHz, and f = 8.78 MHz. This analysis provides a comprehensive characterization of the array’s frequency response, forming a foundation for future multifrequency modulation and applications.

Additionally, for the chirped IDT array comprising 40 units separated by a fixed gap, ensuring the continuity and smoothness of the superpositioned SAW is crucial. A detailed LDV scan was conducted with the starting point at ~3 mm away from the chirped IDT array along the SAW propagation path. The scanning area was 2 mm × 1 mm with a step size of 20 µm. The scanned results of planar SAWs at the four Fresnel ripple peak frequencies from f to f are illustrated in Fig. 2c−f. The x-direction scan spans 1 mm, covering approximately 5 IDT units, while the y-direction scan spans 2 mm, which corresponds to approximately 4𝜆 of the SAWs. As shown in Fig. 2c−f, no obvious misalignment was observed between the SAWs generated by discrete IDT units, confirming that their wavefronts remain collinear. Furthermore, the amplitude of the generated SAWs is uniform, with negligible fluctuations. According to the Huygens–Fresnel principle, each individual unit can be regarded as a point source radiating the secondary wavelet. When multiple units are arranged in close proximity with the interunit gap (10 µm) much smaller than the wavelength (500 µm), the coherent superposition of the secondary wavelets results in a stable, uniform primary wavefront. The minimal interunit gap reduces acoustic energy loss, facilitating the coherent superposition of SAWs from adjacent IDT units. Furthermore, when the input signals to the IDT units are out-of-phase, the corresponding secondary wavelets also maintain a consistent anti-phase relationship, which has been discussed in our previous work [38].

SAW Waveform Modulation. In the standard IDT array, each individual IDT unit enables binary phase modulation of the SAW through the control of its corresponding DPDT switch. By programmably encoding the phase states of the SAWs generated by each IDT unit, various types of the superpositioned SAWs can be achieved, tailored for specific acoustic wave manipulation and control applications. As a demonstration, we generated Airy-type SAWs using the programmable IDT array. Following a similar phase design in our previous work [38], we binarized the Airy function [39], assigning a phase value of 𝜋 to amplitudes greater than 0 and a value of 0 to amplitudes less than 0 [40,41], as depicted in Fig. 3a. The binarized Airy function was then correlated with the spatial phase distribution of the IDT units. Given the limited number of the IDT units (only 40) in our experiment, the number of units assigned to each individual binarized state is illustrated in Fig. 3b. Experiments and simulations were conducted within a 4 cm  2 cm area in front of the IDT array, covering the SAW propagation zone. The experimental and simulation results are shown in Fig. 3c−f, respectively. For clarity, the IDT arrays generating Airy SAWs are highlighted in Fig. 3c and e, with black and white blocks representing the states “1” and “0”, respectively. The digit within each block indicates the number of the IDT units assigned to each state. To simplify the encoding representation, adjacent digits in the sequence correspond to binarized phases 0 and . In Fig. 3c and e, the digit sequences “7, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2” and “2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 7” indicate the arrangement of the IDT unit from the bottom to the top. Upon activation of the IDT array, the generated SAW’s acoustic field was scanned using the LDV. The resulting acoustic field distributions, shown in Fig. 3c and e, exhibit the characteristics bending trajectory of the Airy SAW. Notably, the Airy SAWs in Fig. 3c and e bend in opposite directions due to the reversed digit sequences, confirming the programmable nature of our approach. The corresponding simulation results in Fig. 3d and f closely match the experimental observations validate the accuracy of our encoding method. This programmability offers great flexibility in generating various types of SAWs, expanding potential applications in acoustic wave engineering and related fields. Detailed information regarding the simulation model and parameter settings can be found in Supplementary Note 4.

Spatially Focal Positioning Modulation. The superposition of the curved main lobes from two symmetrical Airy SAWs can generate a focused acoustic field. By positioning two co-axial standard IDT arrays in opposite orientations, a focused standing SAW is formed. In our experiment, we mapped a 2 cm × 1 cm area between the two IDT arrays using the LDV for detailed analysis. The predefined digit sequences encoded in the IDT arrays allow for vertical control of the focal point within the focused standing SAW.

The scanned acoustic field distribution reveals the characteristics of the focused SAW, as shown in Fig. 4a. The encoded digit sequences for both IDT arrays in Fig. 4a are “3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2”. The rationale for the encoded digit sequences can be found in Supplementary Note 5. A distinct focusing effect is observed, with the focal region appearing elongated along the wave propagation direction (x-direction), indicating a notable depth of focus. In contrast, the focal width (lateral resolution) in the perpendicular direction (y-direction) is much narrower. This focused acoustic field forms the basis for controlling particle movement along the y-direction in subsequent experiments. To achieve focal point shifting, the encoding sequence was adjusted by shifting 4 IDT units in the -y direction. The new sequences “2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2” and “2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3,” successfully moved the focal point downward, as demonstrated in Fig. 4b and c. The results show a consistent downward shift of the focal point while maintaining lateral position and focal depth. By extracting the acoustic field distributions along dashed lines A, B, and C, the measured focal displacements d and d were 0.88 mm and 0.96 mm, respectively, closely aligning with the theoretical displacement of 0.92 mm (4 units × 0.23 mm). Simulated acoustic fields (Fig. 4e−g) further validated these findings, with simulated focal displacements l and l measured at 0.9 mm, shown in Fig. 4h. These results confirm that modifying the IDT array encoding sequence enables precise focal point control in the y-direction.

Theoretically, the number of the central IDT units determines the initial position of the main lobe of the Airy SAW and, consequently, the focal point position of the combined focused SAW [42]. To validate this, we altered the encoding sequences to induce lateral focus shifts. The left-side IDT digit sequence was set to “2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2,” while the right-side sequence was “2, 3, 3, 4, 16, 4, 3, 3, 2,” resulting in a leftward focal shift, as shown in Fig. 5a. This shift occurred because fewer central units on the left generated a shorter focal length, while the increased number of units on the right produced a longer focal length. When both sides were symmetrically encoded with the digit sequence “2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 12, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2,” the focal lengths became equal, centering the focal point, as shown in Fig. 5b. Reversing the asymmetry—setting the left and right sequences to “2, 3, 3, 4, 16, 4, 3, 3, 2” and “2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2,” respectively—resulted in a rightward focal shift, symmetric to the first case (Fig. 5c). Cross-sectional acoustic field distributions extracted along dashed lines A, B, and C from Fig. 5a−c, shown in Fig. 5d, indicate focal displacements d₁ and d₂ of approximately 3.91 mm and 3.8 mm, respectively, which closely match the design values. Corresponding simulations (Fig. 5e−g) confirm these results, demonstrating consistent focal shifts. The cross-sectional acoustic intensities along the x-direction (Fig. 5h) reveal lateral displacements l₁ and l₂ of approximately 4 mm, further aligning with the experimental observations. Such dynamic focal position manipulation enabled by programmable IDT array coding can be used for controlled particle movement. The working principle for the particle control and corresponding experimental demonstration are discussed in Supplementary Note 6.

Multifrequency Focal Depth Modulation. By modifying the chirped IDT array’s encoding, with the digit sequence “2, 3, 3, 4, 16, 4, 3, 3, 2”, a focused SAW is generated. The acoustic field distributions of the focused SAWs at four different frequencies were scanned using LDV over a 1.5 cm × 2.5 cm propagation area, with the results shown in Fig. 6a−d. At the frequency of f , the generated SAW exhibits a strong focusing effect, forming an elongated focal spot near the chirped IDT array, as depicted in Fig. 6a. As the frequency increases to f , the focus shifts along the +x direction while maintaining focusing characteristics, as shown in Fig. 6b. At the frequency of f , the focal point shifts along the +x direction, as shown in Fig. 6c. Finally, at the frequency of f , the focal point reaches its farthest position from the IDT array, meanwhile still exhibiting a distinct focusing effect, as seen in Fig. 6d. These results demonstrate that the focus position can be effectively controlled by adjusting the excitation frequency. Cross-sectional profiles along the y- and x-direction at the focal points, indicated by white dashed lines in Fig. 6a−d, are analyzed with the results shown in Fig. 6e and f, respectively. The amplitude values are normalized to the maximum at the focal point. The acoustic field distribution along the y-direction (Fig. 6e) reveals that the focal points at all frequencies overlap, with a focal width of approximately 2𝜆, indicating consistent focus positioning and excellent symmetry. In contrast, along the x-direction (Fig. 6f), the focal position shifts farther from the chirped IDT array as the frequency increases, reaching a maximum displacement of approximately 11 mm. The average full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the focal depth along the x-direction was measured individually for each operating frequency. The obtained values are as follows: 22𝜆 at f₁ = 7.20 MHz, 29𝜆 at f₂ = 7.81 MHz, 28𝜆 at f₃ = 8.35 MHz, and 28𝜆 at f₄ = 8.78 MHz, respectively. This confirms the strong frequency dependence of SAW focusing, enabling precise control over the focal position through frequency tunning. This approach provides a tunable method for concentrating acoustic energy at specific locations, which is highly beneficial for practical applications.

The frequency-dependent focal position of focused SAWs generated by two primary mechanisms. First, within the chirped IDT array, designed with progressively wider finger widths, the generated SAWs with different frequencies are position-dependent: the activation regions for lower and higher frequency SAWs are at the rear and front of the chirped IDT array, respectively. Second, focused SAWs arise from the superposition of symmetric main lobes of Airy SAWs. At higher frequencies, reduced acceleration and main lobe curvature push the focal point further from the source. Together, these mechanisms enable precise frequency-based control of the focal position.

To validate the modulation effect of multi-frequency excitation on the focused SAW, the TDM technique was applied to temporally concatenate four discrete Fresnel ripple peak frequencies, thereby generating TDM waveforms. The technical implementation scheme and corresponding spatial-temporal modulation characteristics are analyzed in Supplementary Note 7. The TDM is generated using MATLAB, and the corresponding code is provided in Supplementary Note 8. The location of the focused energy along the x-axis varies with the operating frequency, as shown in Fig. 6f. The SAW with a higher frequency has a longer focal length from the excitation source. The focal positions of SAWs vary with excitation frequency, leading to distinct energy distributions at each focal point when multifrequency components are superimposed. By adjusting the relative contributions of different frequencies, the focusing effect can be sustained across an extended propagation distance, thereby increasing the focal depth. Since the generated SAWs with frequencies of f₁ (7.20 MHz) and f₄ (8.78 MHz) have the nearest and farthest focal points, respectively, their signal weighting should be enhanced. Meanwhile, the generated SAWs with frequencies of f₂ (7.81 MHz) and f₃ (8.35 MHz) have the focused energy distributions that overlap with those of f₁ and f₄ to a large extent. Therefore, their relative contributions should be minimized to achieve a more uniform energy distribution along the x-axis across the four frequencies, thus extending the effective focal depth. A reference TDM signal with equal cycle allocations (f : f : f : f = 5:5:5:5) serves as a baseline configuration, where each ratio value indicates the number of wavelength cycles per frequency component. LDV scans over a 15 mm × 40 mm propagation area mapped the acoustic field distributions for various TDM configurations (Fig. 7a−e). All tested frequency ratios maintained strong focusing performance while demonstrating progressive focal depth extension. Cross-sectional intensity profiles along the propagation direction (x-axis) extracted from Fig. 7, enable quantitative comparison of focal depth variations across TDM configurations (Fig. 8). These profiles permit systematic evaluation of both focal depth and axial energy distribution for each frequency ratio combination.

The relationship between TDM signal composition and focal depth is quantified using FWHM analysis of the acoustic field profiles, as shown in Fig. 8. Increasing the proportion of f (8.78 MHz) from the baseline (5:5:5:5) to an optimized configuration (5:0:4:11) ratios results in the focal depth extension from 40λ to 43λ by temporally stitching the acoustic fields of generated SAWs with different frequencies. However, excessive f weighting reduces the focal depth to 27λ due to diminished near-field contributions from f (7.20 MHz). This nonlinear behavior results from unbalanced energy distribution: a dominant f components amplifies distal focusing but weakens proximal intensity, disrupting superposition across the extended focal depth. For the frequency combination of (5:0:4:11), the SAW energy assigned to the frequency of f₂ is 0, meaning that the f₂-frequency SAW has no contribution. This is likely because the f₂-frequency SAW energy distribution overlaps with those of f₁ and f₃, while its peak is higher than that of f₃ (see Fig. 6f). Therefore, to extend the focal depth, our proposed frequency-weighting strategy is to suppress f₂ and f₃ while increase f₄. As a result, we experimentally optimized (5:0:4:11) ratio to achieve the extended focal depth of 43λ with uniform energy distribution.

---

## Methods

Simulation. Numerical simulations were performed using the Piezoelectricity module in COMSOL Multiphysics. A two-dimensional model of a 128° Y-X cut LiNbO₃ substrate was constructed to reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy. Perfectly matched layers (PMLs) with a thickness of approximately one wavelength (500 μm) were applied around the substrate to absorb boundary reflections. The IDT array electrodes were modelled on the substrate surface and excited with either in-phase or out-of-phase voltage signals (20 Vₚₚ) to control the acoustic phase. The resulting acoustic field distributions were visualized by plotting the displacement field.

Experiment. The IDT arrays were fabricated on a 128° Y-X cut LiNbO₃ substrate using standard photolithography, followed by deposition of a 3-nm Cr adhesion layer and a 50-nm Au electrode layer via electron beam evaporation. The arrays consist of 40 independently addressable IDT units, each connected to a control module equipped with DPDT switches for binary phase inversion. SAWs were generated by applying AC signals (20 Vₚₚ, 7.98 MHz for standard IDTs; 5–12 MHz swept for chirped IDTs) from a signal generator (DG4102, Rigol, China). The out-of-plane displacement fields of propagating SAWs were measured using a LDV (PSV-500 Scanning Head, Polytec, Germany). The entire setup was mounted on a two-axis stepper motor translation stage with 10 μm positioning resolution.
